2027-06-17.title: Fifth Thursday of the Apostles
2027-06-17.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Called to share the glory of Christ
2027-06-17.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven.
2027-06-17.verse: It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is useless. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.
theo: The Second Letter of Peter opens with one of the boldest sentences in the New Testament: “His divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and goodness. Thus he has given us, through these things, his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may escape from the corruption that is in the world because of lust, and may become participants of the divine nature.” Participants of the divine nature: the Christian vocation is not only to be forgiven, nor only to be good, but to share in the very life of God. The Eastern Churches, our own among them, have always loved this verse. The Fathers summed it up in a famous phrase (in substance): the Son of God became what we are so that we might become what he is, not by nature but by grace. We do not cease to be creatures; we are taken up into the communion of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as iron placed in the fire glows with the fire's heat while remaining iron. This happens first in Baptism, grows through the sacraments, above all the Holy Qurbana, and will be complete in glory.

Because God has given so much, Peter says, our response must be wholehearted: “For this very reason, you must make every effort to support your faith with goodness, and goodness with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with endurance, and endurance with godliness, and godliness with mutual affection, and mutual affection with love.” It is like a ladder, or like a chain in which each link holds the next. It begins with faith, the gift we received at the font, and it ends with love, the greatest gift. Between them stand the ordinary virtues of a Christian life: goodness in conduct, knowledge of the faith, self-control of tongue and appetite, endurance in trouble, godliness in prayer, the warm affection of brothers and sisters, and finally love that reaches even enemies. Grace and effort are not rivals here. God gives everything needed, and we must “make every effort.” Where these virtues are growing, Peter says, they “keep you from being ineffective and unfruitful.” And the one who lacks them “is short-sighted and blind, and is forgetful of the cleansing of past sins.” To forget our Baptism is to forget who we are.

The Gospel brings us to the end of the discourse on the bread of life. Jesus has said, “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life” (John 6:54), and many of his disciples are shaken: “This teaching is difficult; who can accept it?” Jesus does not soften his words. He asks, “Does this offend you? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” and adds, “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is useless. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” He is not taking back what he said about his flesh as true food. He is answering a crude, merely human way of hearing it, as if he meant pieces of meat. The flesh he gives is the flesh of the Son of Man who will ascend to the Father, filled with the life-giving Spirit. On its own, human understanding profits nothing here; only the Spirit opens the mystery. That is why, in the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, the priest prays that the Holy Spirit may come and rest upon the offering. Many disciples turned back that day (John 6:66), but Peter answered for the Twelve: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). Here the two readings meet. We become participants of the divine nature above all by receiving, in the Spirit, the Body and Blood of the Son of God, and each Communion is meant to lift us one rung higher on Peter's ladder, from faith toward love.
outline: Ask: do I know that I am called to share the life of God himself?
Point 1 · Participants of the divine nature
God's power gives everything needed; becoming by grace what he is by nature.
Point 2 · From faith to love, rung by rung
Peter's ladder of virtues; grace and every effort.
A hard teaching, the flesh of the Son of Man, Peter's answer.

live: Choose the rung of Peter's ladder where you are weakest, perhaps self-control or endurance, and practise it consciously each day this week.
Before your next Holy Qurbana, spend five quiet minutes asking the Holy Spirit to open your heart to the mystery you will receive.
fathers: The Word of God became man so that we might be made God: he showed himself through a body so that we might come to know the unseen Father, and he endured the insults of men so that we might inherit immortality. What he is by nature, we become by grace.

They understood his flesh as flesh is cut up in a corpse or sold in the market, not as it is quickened by the Spirit. The flesh profits nothing, he says, but only when it is alone; let the Spirit come to the flesh, as love comes to knowledge, and it profits very much. Otherwise the Word would not have become flesh to dwell among us.
magis: The Word became flesh to make us partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4); as St Athanasius says, the Son of God became man so that we might become God, and St Thomas Aquinas: the only-begotten Son, wanting to make us sharers in his divinity, assumed our nature, so that he, made man, might make men gods.

The first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalised them: this is a hard saying; who can listen to it? The Eucharist and the Cross are stumbling blocks, and the question, will you also go away?, echoes through the ages as a loving invitation to discover that only he has the words of eternal life.

A virtue is a habitual and firm disposition to do the good; the human virtues, acquired by effort and purified and elevated by divine grace, make possible ease, self-mastery and joy in leading a morally good life.
saints: No saint's memorial is kept in the Syro-Malabar or the Latin calendar today. In the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church it is the second day of the Apostles' Fast.

13–18 June: the fifth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles (in the Latin calendar the memorial of St Antony of Padua gives way to the Sunday). Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius are listed in the calendar. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Ahead: Thu 24 June, the Birth of John the Baptist; Tue 29 June, Sts Peter and Paul, a day of obligation.
2027-06-17.prayer: Father, by your divine power you have given us everything needed for life and godliness, and you have called us to share your own divine nature. Holy Spirit, who gives life, open our hearts to the words of Jesus, which are spirit and life, and come upon the offering of our Holy Qurbana. Lord Jesus, when your teaching is hard, keep us from turning back, and let us say with Peter: to whom can we go? Help us to make every effort to add to our faith goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, mutual affection and love. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Spirit who gives life comes upon the bread and wine, and they become the Body and Blood of the Son of Man who ascended to the Father. Receiving him, we become partakers of the divine nature.
The words of the anaphora are spirit and life. Whoever listens to them with faith and receives the Lord with love climbs, Sunday by Sunday and day by day, from faith to love.

2027-06-17.action: Practise the virtue you most lack each day this week, and pray to the Holy Spirit before your next Holy Qurbana.
2027-06-17.question: Which rung of Peter's ladder am I standing on, and which have I skipped?

family.explain: Saint Peter gives us a ladder to climb. At the bottom is faith, which we received at Baptism. Then come goodness, learning about God, self-control (not always doing what we feel like), patience, prayer, loving our brothers and sisters, and at the very top, love for everyone. God helps us climb, but we must also try hard. And Jesus helps us most of all when we receive him in Holy Communion.
family.intention: We pray for children preparing for their First Holy Communion, and for all who find the faith hard to accept.
family.ask: Ask: “Which step of the ladder is hardest for each of us? Let us help one another with it this week.”

illus: An old carpenter near Changanassery was asked by the parish to make a new wooden ladder for the choir loft. His grandson, home for the school holidays, helped him. As they fixed each rung, the old man named it: ‘This one is faith. This one is goodness. This one is knowing your catechism. This one is controlling your tongue.’ The boy laughed and asked what the top rung was. ‘Love,’ said the grandfather. ‘And remember: if one rung in the middle is missing or loose, you will not get to the top safely. You cannot jump from faith to love and skip self-control.’ Years later, when the grandson was a seminarian, he read the first chapter of the Second Letter of Peter and recognised the ladder. He still has the carpenter's pencil his grandfather used to mark the rungs.

pm.open: Holy Spirit, you give life; the words of Jesus are spirit and life. Open our ears and our hearts as we pray, and lift us up to share the life of God. Amen.
share: His divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3). Do I believe that God has already given me what I need to be holy?
You may become participants of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). How does this calling change the way I see myself?
Support your faith with goodness… and mutual affection with love (2 Peter 1:5–7). Which virtue do I most need to grow in?
This teaching is difficult; who can accept it? (John 6:60). Which teaching of Jesus do I find hardest, and do I still stay with him?
pm.resp: Lord, you have the words of eternal life.
interc: For the Church in this Season of the Apostles, that she may lead all people to share the life of God.
For those who find the Church's teaching on the Eucharist hard to accept, that the Spirit may open their hearts.
For children preparing for First Holy Communion and for their catechists.
For those struggling with addictions, that they may grow in self-control and endurance.
For our parish, that we may support our faith with goodness, knowledge and love.
pm.close: Father, you call us to share your divine nature through your Son and in the Spirit who gives life. Help us to make every effort to grow from faith to love, and keep us faithful when his teaching is hard, for he alone has the words of eternal life. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Saint Peter tells us something astonishing: God has called us to “become participants of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4). Not just to be forgiven, not just to be good people, but to share the very life of God. That is our dignity as baptised Christians.

God has given us everything we need. But Peter says we must also “make every effort.” He gives us a ladder: faith, then goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, mutual affection, and at the top, love (2 Peter 1:5–7). We cannot skip the rungs in the middle.

In the Gospel, many disciples find Jesus' teaching about eating his flesh and drinking his blood too hard: “This teaching is difficult; who can accept it?” Jesus does not change his words. He says: “It is the spirit that gives life… The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63). Only the Holy Spirit can open our hearts to this mystery.

Many turned away that day. But Peter said: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.” When something in our faith is hard, let us not walk away. Let us stay with Jesus and ask the Spirit for light.

Every time we receive the Holy Qurbana, we receive the Body and Blood of the Son of God, and we share more deeply in God's own life. So let us climb Peter's ladder, rung by rung, from faith to love. Amen.
kids: Children, Saint Peter gives us a ladder. The first step is faith. Then come being good, learning about God, controlling ourselves, being patient, praying, loving our family, and at the very top, loving everyone! This week, try to climb one step higher. And remember: in Holy Communion Jesus gives himself to help you climb.
